A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching retained results across renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 11 benchmark-prediction methods across 19 benchmarks, including interpolation, extrapolation, model-similarity analyses, ablations, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds smaller-budget experiments, ranking-preservation results, and alternative source–target model splits.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 and Appendix A retain the same methods, estimator equations, regression procedures, and PCA algorithm. Revised AIPW scores are not accompanied by a documented algorithmic or implementation change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 19 benchmarks from HELM-Lite, GLUE, OpenLLM, and ImageNet, with the same underlying model pools. The additional experiments change budgets, model partitions, or evaluation criteria within this coverage.

E2.justification: The same 11 methods participate in the retained comparisons and the new analyses. No evaluated comparator is added or removed; newly cited research does not enter the experimental comparator set.

E3.justification: v2 substantially expands evaluation protocols: core-set sizes 10 and 20 supplement 50, 100, and 200; ranking preservation is measured with Kendall’s tau; and Appendix C.4 adds interpolation with only 10 source models and near extrapolation using bottom-75% sources and top-25% targets. The original primary splits remain.

E4.justification: Beyond extending the core-set-size ablation, v2 adds analyses testing whether predictions preserve rankings, whether methods withstand scarce source-model data, and whether extrapolation failures persist with a smaller source–target gap. Table 3 and Figures 16–17 address substantive questions absent from v1.

E5.justification: Both versions already report 100 random trials and appendix standard errors. v2 continues this reporting practice and averages ranking results over 100 trials. Changed standard-error values and additional result rows do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New budget, ranking, and alternative-split results substantially expand the empirical record. Under retained settings, Table 1 changes AIPW’s mean gap at n=200 from 1.8% to 1.5% for interpolation and 2.0% to 1.8% for extrapolation. Its n=50 extrapolation wins increase from 18 to all 19 benchmarks. Figures 2–4 and corresponding appendix figures also revise AIPW entries, correlations, and aggregate reduction percentages.

T1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds a cited necessary-and-sufficient correlation-threshold condition for AIPW to outperform random sampling. This is a limited theoretical qualification without an explicit threshold formula or proof; the existing estimator equations, bounds, and mathematical definitions remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: simple regression baselines challenge careful subset selection, prediction depends on model similarity, extrapolation undermines most methods, and AIPW offers qualified benefits. Additional experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 reverses an important interpretation: v1 says AIPW’s relative advantage diminishes with increasing core-set size, whereas v2 says it remains stable and depends on prediction quality. v2 also removes the discussion of Anchor-Points-Predictor’s large-core-set failures and adds interpretations of ranking preservation and alternative model splits.

D1.justification: The implementation descriptions, PCA component choices, random-search budget, benchmark-processing information, runtime measurements, and code/data access information are retained. v2 supplies protocols for its new analyses but does not disclose an implementation explanation for the revised AIPW results.

R1.justification: v2 adds four cited works concerning metabench, lifelong model evaluation, prompt best-arm identification, and non-asymptotic prediction-powered inference. It adds a distinction between benchmark prediction and best-model identification, plus the AIPW correlation qualification, while retaining the overall research positioning.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence remain intact. Local changes include a model-similarity subheading, rewriting Section 4.5, organizing Appendix C into four subsections, moving acknowledgments, and correcting the introductory minimum model count from 84 to 83, consistent with the existing setup.

P2.justification: The evidence displays are substantially expanded with a ranking table and six additional heatmaps. Table 1 is redesigned to include five budgets per regime, remove reduction subcolumns, and highlight minima. Retained appendix heatmaps are renumbered, while tables, captions, and several figure sizes are adjusted.

improvement.justification: The new ranking and alternative-split analyses test whether the earlier conclusions depend on the evaluation metric, abundant source models, or an unusually large extrapolation gap, providing useful additional support. The gain is limited by unexplained AIPW revisions and inconsistent numerical summaries: v2 Section 4.3 still reports a 185.1% increase for Random-Search-Learn, although Figure 3 now shows 177.5%. These issues prevent a stronger overall improvement judgment.
